theme: The reversal; deliverance; Purim, God unseen but sovereign
readingInstruction: Read Esther 8:1-10:3. The decree is reversed, the Jews defend themselves, and the festival of Purim is established. Read for the language of reversal.
settingTheScene: Haman is dead, but the first decree, written in the king’s name, cannot be revoked under Persian law. Esther and Mordecai are authorized to write a second decree, allowing the Jews to defend themselves on the appointed day. The book ends with the establishment of the festival of Purim, still celebrated by Jews today, and a brief note on Mordecai’s greatness.
observation: “On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman” (8:1).
“And Mordecai… was set over the house of Haman” (8:2).
“For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people?” (8:6).
“The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor” (8:16).
“And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them” (8:17).
“On the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain mastery over them, the reverse occurred” (9:1).
“As the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness” (9:22).
“For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus… seeking the welfare of his people and speaking peace to all his people” (10:3).
interpretation:
The second half of the book is a great reversal. What was meant for evil is turned to good. The day appointed for the destruction of the Jews becomes a day of their deliverance. The man who sought the throne’s favor hangs on his own gallows. The man who would have been executed wears the king’s ring. Mourning becomes feasting. Fear falls on the enemies.

The Jews are allowed to defend themselves, which they do. The text insists that they “laid no hand on the plunder,” emphasizing that they were not seeking gain, in contrast to the Amalekite conflict where Saul kept the spoil. This time, the enemy of God’s people is finished, and the people do what Saul failed to do.

Purim, from “pur,” the lot, is established as a perennial reminder. “The month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness.” The feast would include sending gifts to one another and to the poor. The memory of deliverance becomes an act of generosity.

Why is God never named? Many see a theological point. The book is written for the diaspora, the Jews who stayed behind. They would have to live by faith without temple or prophet. Esther shows them that God’s providence is not limited to Jerusalem. He works through palaces, sleepless nights, banquets, and edicts. He keeps his promise to preserve the line of Abraham, through which the Messiah would come. The Jewish people cannot be wiped out, because the seed of the woman must come.

The last verse describes Mordecai as one who “sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.” It is a picture of faithful service in a foreign court, much like Joseph and Daniel before him.
connection: Romans 8:31: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Isaiah 61:3 promises a garland instead of ashes. John 16:20: “Your sorrow will turn into joy.” Psalm 30:11: “You have turned for me my mourning into dancing.” Jeremiah 29:7 told the exiles to seek the welfare of the city. Galatians 4:4: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son.” The preservation of the Jews led to the birth of Jesus.
application:
Think about a situation that seems hopeless. Ask God for the “reversal” he can bring.

Practice the spirit of Purim: send a gift to a friend and to someone in need.

Seek the welfare of your city or workplace, as Mordecai did.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for turning sorrow into gladness.
Thank him for preserving his people when his name is unseen.
Ask him to make you glad and generous.
